subjective.citation_text: Patient: Hi, I'm Joe, and I'm 32 years old. I came in because I hurt my right knee while skiing over the weekend. It feels swollen and painful, and I heard a pop when it happened. I've been taking some Advil and icing it, but I wanted to get checked out. Doctor: Have you experienced any instability, locking, or difficulty bearing weight on the right knee since the injury? Patient: I haven't had any real instability, but it's been pretty painful to put weight on it. I've been able to walk a little, but it's swollen and feels tight. I didn't really lock up or anything like that. Doctor: Have you noticed any locking, clicking, or giving way of the knee? Have you been able to fully bend or straighten the knee? Patient: I haven't noticed any locking or clicking, but I did feel a pop when it happened. As for bending or straightening, I can get through the full range of motion, but it feels tight and hurts a little when I do. Doctor: Could you describe the exact mechanism of the injury, such as whether you twisted your knee, landed awkwardly, or collided with something while skiing? Patient: Sure, I was skiing with some friends, and it was snowing pretty hard. I couldn't really see well, and the two paths kind of came together. I think the front end of my skis dug into the snow, and I ended up doing a cartwheel but kind of stopped halfway through. I could feel a pop in my right knee right then, and the pain came right after that. Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging studies such as X-rays or MRI for your knee injury, and if so, what were the findings? Patient: I haven't had any imaging studies done yet for my knee. The doctor did mention that there was no fracture or bony abnormality on the X-ray, but I don't know the full details of the results. I'm just here getting checked out today.

The patient is a 32-year-old male with acute right knee pain following a skiing injury. He reported a popping sound at the time of injury, followed by swelling, pain, and difficulty bearing weight. The absence of numbness, tingling, or weakness suggests no significant nerve involvement. The presence of swelling, bruising, and tenderness, along with pain on weight-bearing, supports a soft tissue injury. The differential diagnoses include: 1) MCL sprain, which is common in valgus stress injuries and can present with pain, swelling, and tenderness along the medial joint line; 2) meniscal tear, which can occur with twisting injuries and may present with pain, swelling, and a sensation of tightness; 3) patellar tendinitis, which can occur with overuse or direct trauma and may present with localized pain and tightness. The patient has no prior knee injuries or surgeries, which reduces the likelihood of chronic conditions. The absence of locking or giving way suggests that the cruciate ligaments may not be involved. The lack of imaging studies limits the ability to confirm the diagnosis definitively.

Medication: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for pain and inflammation; acetaminophen as an alternative if contraindicated. 3.
